title: The US Just Found a New Legal Route to Tariff India. This Time, It May Stick.
excerpt: After two court defeats killed Trump's emergency tariffs, USTR Jamieson Greer is using a forced labor investigation to impose a 12.5% surcharge on Indian goods — with no expiration date and no cap.
body:
The Trump administration has found a new legal mechanism to impose tariffs on India — and this one is built to survive the courts. For the vast Indian diaspora in the US, UK, and Canada, these escalating trade tensions carry significant implications, potentially impacting family businesses, investment flows, and the cost of goods imported from India.

After the Supreme Court struck down emergency-based universal tariffs in February, and a trade court killed a follow-up 10% levy under Section 122 in May, the Office of the United States Trade Representative has pivoted to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. A 98-page report published last week concludes that 60 economies, including India, have failed to prohibit imports of goods produced with forced labor. The proposed penalty: a 12.5% tariff on Indian goods, with no statutory expiration date and no maximum percentage cap.

## Why This Is Different

Section 301 is the same legal tool the US used to impose tariffs on China during Trump's first term — tariffs that survived every legal challenge and remain in effect years later. Unlike the emergency powers the courts rejected, Section 301 gives the executive branch broad, durable authority to act against foreign trade practices deemed "unreasonable."

The forced labor framing is strategic. The investigation, launched in March 2026, covers economies responsible for 99.4% of US imports. India is among 54 economies that the USTR says have no legal prohibition on importing goods made with forced labor. Six others — including the EU, Canada, and Mexico — have laws but allegedly fail to enforce them. Those nations face a lower 10% rate.

"For nearly a century, the United States has prohibited the importation of goods made with forced labor. It is time for our trading partners to follow suit," Ambassador Jamieson Greer said in the report.

## The Trade Deal Complication

The timing is not accidental. India and the US are deep in negotiations for a bilateral trade agreement, with Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal indicating an interim deal could land by mid-July. The Section 301 tariff is now part of that negotiation.

"This is certainly an element of the negotiation," said Atul Keshap, president of the US-India Business Council, who described the overall trade deal as "75 years overdue." He urged both sides to close quickly so trade could reach "the $500 billion mark," which he called "woefully underpowered" today.

An Indian trade official told Reuters on Monday that the bilateral deal can be finalised only after the Section 301 process concludes, and that India would seek assurances it will not face additional tariffs after signing.

## The Expert Pushback

Not everyone in New Delhi is willing to accept the tariff as a negotiating chip. WTO expert Mukesh Bhatnagar called the forced labor rationale "specious" and argued the tariffs violate global trade rules. "This must be contested upfront and challenged in the WTO if actually applied," he said.
